Napoleons Wine

By: ALTYDVRYSTAAT PRODUCTIONS | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Napoleons Wine, sold to the highest bidder.

Unique Selling Point:
Footage of re-corcking and the auction of the 1821 Grand Constance wine.

Summary:
On 22 May a bottle of 1821 Grand Constance, from a batch that was supposed to be shipped to Napoleon in exile on St. Helena, was sold at a rare wine auction in Stellenbosch for R420 000.00 after the auctioneers initially thought it would fetch between R80000.00 and R130000.00

It was re-corked two years ago (great footage of this very intricate process) in anticipation of the auction that had to be postponed last year due to lockdown restrictions.

Can a bottle of wine ever be worth this much? What is this wine that Napoleon demanded while in exile and that authors such as Jane Austin and Charles Dickens wrote about.
And who bought it and what do they plan to do with it at more than R1000 per milliliter?

Script:


V/O The island of St Helena...
V/O It was here at Longwood House where the exiled French emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte spent the last 6 years of his life...
V/O Having once been the most powerful man in the world, he was used to the finer things in life, and even here he dined lavishly and enjoyed a fine vintage...
Joanne Gibson He was a big fan of Chambertin, he loved his burgundy, he loved his champagne… but he absolutely loved Constantia.
V/O Grand Constance, an unfortified dessert wine, was said to satisfy Napoleon’s sweet tooth… According to wine journalist Joanne Gibson, more than a thousand litres of this wine was shipped to St Helena every year.
Joanne Gibson His former aide, Emmanuel, the Comte de Las Cases, he ended up at the Cape after being found to be smuggling letters to Europe, plotting Napoleon's escape. So he was banished to the Cape. And while he was here, he arranged some shipments to Napoleon and Napoleon drank up to a bottle a day.
LINK South Africa’s first wine farm, Constantia was established in 1685 by Simon van der Stel. He loved the scenery, the climate and especially the rich soil. And within a mere century Constantia wines were being served at the most distinguished dinner tables across Europe.

V/o Constantia wine, or Constance as it was known in Europe, is even mentioned in Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility as a cure for a broken heart.
Boela Gerber There are a lot of famous people that drank the old Grand Contance over the centuries.

V/O Today, Groot Constantia winemaker Boela Gerber is following in the footsteps of Hendrik Cloete who made the estate famous more than 200 years ago.
Boela Gerber The VOC officer that was in charge of procurement for St Helena, he was married to one of the Cloete's daughters, so he got the wine from his father-in-law to give to Napoleon.
V/O And Napoleon’s love for Grand Constance was unmistakable until his end in May 1821.
Joanne Gibson On his deathbed he refused to take anything else - no other food, no other drink… but he asked for a glass of Constantia wine.
LINK There have been some notable collectors of Constantia wines over the centuries. According to the cellar book at Versailles in 1782 Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette had more Constantia in their collection than Burgundy -- around 2,500 bottles ---
V/O Today there are said to be 12 bottles left of 1821 Grand Constance, part of a consignment that was likely destined for St Helena…
Joanne Napoleon did die in May 1821 so that wine would still have been fermenting probably. A good amount of it was probably earmarked for him because for five or six years, St Helena had been the destination for a lot of Constantia… Certainly after he died, there was a little bit more to go around.
V/O 3 bottles of 1821 Gand Constance have been tucked away in the Distill Tabernacle cellar in Stellenbosch after they were bought at an auction in London in 1980.
Niel Groenewald We knew of its exceptional value at the label being French, being made for Napoleon Bonaparte because he was quite a big fan of the wine.
V/O For the past 4 decades winemaker Niel Groenewald has been keeping an eye on the treasured vintage and finally in 2019 they made the decision to sell a single bottle… but no-one was sure if the wine was still drinkable...
LINK After having survived almost 200 years, it was decided to embark on a delicate recorking process to ensure that Grand Constance 1821 is preserved for years to come...
Niel Groenewald It actually enhances the value because it gives somebody with pretty good credentials, gives them time to also taste the wine and see if it's still sound after all these years.
V/O For a process this delicate they needed the expertise of cork specialist Joaquim Sá and master sommelier, Jean-Vincent Ridon...
UPSOUND I’m scared that the cork will fall through now. I’m scared that when we close it the bottle explodes… I have no… there’s no plan B...
Joaquim Sa When you open it, you don't know what you're going to find. And the magic of this operation was that once you open the cork, the air of the room immediately got filled up with these spiciness and caramel,
Derek: 200 years of it…
200 years of it.
Derek: Did you get a sip of the wine?
Yes, I'm one of the few, apart from Napoleon that had the privilege to taste it a few times. It's really, really unique. It's the most incredible wine I've ever tasted before.
V/O With very little knowledge -- compared to today -- the winemakers managed to make something quite unique, says Gerber...
Boela Gerber It’s a bit of an enigma. I know that the guys did sulphur their wines, but very inefficient way of sulphuring it. So, it just seems that the combination of the alcohol and the sugar allowed the wine to be still drinkable after 200 years.
V/O Once the bottle is opened they insert Argon gas to prevent the wine from being exposed to the air.
UPSOUND At least I can smell a bit of it…
V/O The most nerve-wracking part of the operation is re-inserting the new cork into a 200-year old hand-made glass bottle.
Joaquim Sa They used to blow the glass into a mold and then they would use some tools to shape the bottle.
V/O This means that every bottle has a differently shaped neck and Sa had to carve a specific tapered cork to fit each of the bottles.
Joaquim Sa We had to hand cork it actually. So, compress it and then insert it very slowly, praying that the bottle won't collapse.
Derek: Won’t break.
Exactly, because it would be quite an expensive accident...
UPSOUND Voila”
V/o Ready to last another 200 years, one of the recorked bottles finally made its way to the Cape Fine and Rare Wine Auction in May this year...
Niel Groenewald We had a reserve price in the catalogue for R80,000 rand… and we were hoping for at least 130.
V/O Within seconds it became clear that everyone’s expectations would be exceeded.
Auction Sold R420,000
Joanne Gibson I was so excited. Yeah. I'm actually a bit shocked...
Niel Groenewald I'm still getting goosebumps. And I just think of the hype and you just see the number climbing and climbing. And it just really reiterates again what beautiful gems we've got in South Africa.
Boela Gerber Derek: Boela, can you understand somebody paying more than 400000 for a bottle of wine?
On a winemaker's salary it doesn't make sense at all, but if you have the cash, if you have the cash, it is history. I mean, it's it's it's not only about the liquid. Can you imagine what that wine has seen, what happened to the world over the last two hundred years while that wine's been sitting in a glass bottle. So if I had the cash, I would have bought it in a flash, I promise you.
V/O While the auctioned bottle of 1821 Grand Constance makes its way to its new home somewhere in the UK, one can only speculate about its future. Perhaps it will be reserved for a grand occasion, or maybe it will once again raise eyebrows at an exclusive wine auction in 200 years from now...
Niel Groenewald Derek: Now we've got another bottle or two of the 1821, haven't you.
We bought three. And so we've got some. And one was used to fill up the other two. So there is still one full bottle with the best looking label and then there's a half a bottle.
Derek: So shouldn't we be trying some now?
We could be trying some, but then I would need to send you a bill.


PROMO 1 How much would you be willing to pay for a rare bottle of wine that was destined for the exiled French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte 200 years ago? 100,000… or maybe 400,000 rand?

PROMO 2 On his deathbed 200 years ago Napoleon insisted on a glass of his favourite wine from Groot Constantia, but what would a bottle be worth today, if you can get your hands on one?

PROMO 3 A bottle of Grand Constance, once a firm favourite of European nobility, recently came under the hammer and sold for a staggering R420,000. We take a look at its 200-year history.
